# Class

- A Class is a user-defined data type that groups data members and member functions into a single unit.
- It serves as a blueprint for creating objects and supports Object-Oriented Programming (OOP).
- Syntax: `class ClassName { access_specifier: data_members; member_functions(); };`
- Example: `class Student { public: int id; char grade; void display(); };`

# Components of a Class

- Data Members: Variables declared inside a class.
- Member Functions: Functions declared inside a class.
- Access Specifiers: Control access to class members.

# Access Specifiers

- Public: Members can be accessed from anywhere.
- Private: Members can be accessed only within the class.
- Protected: Members can be accessed within the class and derived classes.

# Creating Multiple Objects

- Each object has its own copy of data members.
- Example: `Student s1, s2, s3;`

# Class vs Object

- Class: Logical entity, blueprint for creating objects.
- Object: Physical entity, instance of a class.

# Advantages of Classes

- Encapsulation of data and functions.
- Code reusability.
- Improved security through data hiding.
- Better program organization.
- Supports Object-Oriented Programming.

# Applications

- Student Management Systems
- Banking Applications
- Inventory Systems
- Healthcare Systems
- Software Development

# Object

- An object is an instance of a class that occupies memory.
- It is used to access data members and member functions of a class.
- A class is a blueprint, while an object is the actual implementation of that blueprint.
- Syntax: `ClassName objectName;`
- Example: `Student s1;` (Student → Class, s1 → Object)
- The dot (.) operator is used to access data members and member functions.
- Example: `s1.id = 101;` and `s1.display();`
- Each object has its own separate copy of data members.
- Characteristics of objects:
  - Occupy memory.
  - Have state (data members).
  - Have behavior (member functions).
  - Are created from classes.
  - Can interact with other objects.
- Creating multiple objects: `Student s1, s2, s3;`
- Advantages of objects:
  - Represent real-world entities.
  - Support data encapsulation.
  - Improve code reusability.
  - Simplify program design.
  - Enable object-oriented programming.
- Applications of objects:
  - Student Management Systems
  - Banking Systems
  - Library Management Systems
  - Inventory Systems
  - Hospital Management Systems
- An object is the fundamental runtime entity in Object-Oriented Programming.

# Instantiation

- Instantiation is the process of creating an object from a class.
- A class is only a blueprint, and instantiation creates the actual object that can be used in a program.
- Syntax: `ClassName objectName;`
- Example: `class Student { public: int id; }; Student s1;`
- Creating `s1` is called Instantiation.
- A class itself does not occupy memory for its data members.
- Memory is allocated only when objects are created.
- Objects allow access to data members and member functions.
- Two separate objects are created: `Student s1; Student s2;`
- Each object has its own copy of data members.
- Instantiation allocates memory for data members.
- Instantiation creates usable objects from classes.
- Instantiation supports object-oriented programming.
- Instantiation allows multiple objects from the same class.
- When an object is instantiated, memory is allocated and the object can access the data members and member functions defined in the class.
- Instantiation is necessary for accessing data members and member functions.
- Multiple instantiations are possible: `Student s1; Student s2; Student s3;`
- Each object has its own memory allocation.
- Instantiation is the process of creating an object from a class, allocating memory, and making it usable.

# Inheritance

- Inheritance is an Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) feature that allows a new class to acquire the properties and behaviors of an existing class.
- The existing class is called the Base Class (Parent Class), and the new class is called the Derived Class (Child Class).
- Inheritance promotes code reusability and reduces redundancy.
- Syntax: `class Derived : public Base { };`
- Example Program: A `Student` class inherits the `show()` function from the `Person` class.

## Types of Inheritance

- Single Inheritance: One derived class inherits from one base class.
- Multilevel Inheritance: A class inherits from another derived class.
- Multiple Inheritance: A class inherits from more than one base class.
- Hierarchical Inheritance: Multiple derived classes inherit from the same base class.
- Hybrid Inheritance: Combination of two or more inheritance types.

## Access Modes in Inheritance

- Public Inheritance: Public members remain public, protected members remain protected.
- Protected Inheritance: Protected members remain protected, public members become protected.
- Private Inheritance: All members become private.

## Advantages

- Code reusability.
- Reduces code duplication.
- Easier maintenance.
- Supports extensibility.
- Represents real-world relationships.

## Inheritance vs Composition

- Inheritance: "is-a" relationship, child acquires parent properties.
- Composition: "has-a" relationship, class contains another class.

## Exam Point

- Inheritance is an OOP mechanism that improves code reusability and supports hierarchical classification.

# Encapsulation

- Encapsulation is the process of combining data and methods into a single unit called a class, while restricting direct access to the data.
- It is one of the fundamental principles of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) and is also known as data hiding.
- Purpose of Encapsulation: Protect data from unauthorized access, improve security, increase maintainability, and control how data is accessed and modified.
- Access Specifiers:
  - Private: Accessible only within the class.
  - Public: Accessible from anywhere.
  - Protected: Accessible within the class and derived classes.
- Advantages of Encapsulation: Data security, data hiding, better control over data, improved code maintainability, and increased modularity.
- Real-Life Example: Bank Account, where a user can deposit and withdraw money but cannot directly access or modify the account balance.
- Encapsulation vs Abstraction:
  - Encapsulation: Hides data, achieved using classes and access specifiers, focuses on data security.
  - Abstraction: Hides implementation details, focuses on showing only essential features.
- Exam Point: Encapsulation is the OOP concept of binding data members and member functions into a single unit (class) and restricting direct access to data using access specifiers.
- It is used to achieve data hiding and security.
- Example in C++: Using a class with private data and public methods to set and get the data.
- Characteristics of Encapsulation: Binding data and methods into a single unit, restricting direct access to data, and improving data security.
- Types of Access Specifiers: Private, Public, and Protected.
- Components of Encapsulation: Data and methods.
- Example of Encapsulation: Bank Account, where the account balance is hidden and can only be accessed through deposit and withdrawal methods.
- Applications of Encapsulation: Improving code maintainability, increasing modularity, and enhancing data security.
- Steps to implement Encapsulation: Define a class with private data and public methods to access and modify the data.
- Comparison of Encapsulation and Abstraction: Encapsulation focuses on data security, while Abstraction focuses on hiding implementation details.

# Polymorphism

- Polymorphism is an Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) concept that allows the same function or operator to behave differently in different situations.
- It is also known as "many forms".
- Types of Polymorphism: Compile-Time Polymorphism and Run-Time Polymorphism.
- Compile-Time Polymorphism is achieved during compilation.
- Run-Time Polymorphism is achieved during program execution.
- Compile-Time Polymorphism includes Function Overloading and Operator Overloading.
- Function Overloading: Same function name with different parameters.
- Operator Overloading: Existing operators are given new meanings.
- Run-Time Polymorphism includes Inheritance, Virtual Functions, and Function Overriding.
- Virtual Function: A function declared using the virtual keyword in the base class.
- Advantages of Polymorphism: Code reusability, Flexibility, Easier maintenance, Extensibility, and Support for dynamic binding.
- Real-Life Example: Shape with different implementations (Circle, Rectangle, Triangle).
- Compile-Time vs Run-Time Polymorphism: Compile-Time Polymorphism is faster and uses static binding, while Run-Time Polymorphism is slightly slower and uses dynamic binding.
- Polymorphism is the ability of an object or function to take many forms.
- It is of two types: Compile-Time Polymorphism (Function Overloading, Operator Overloading) and Run-Time Polymorphism (Function Overriding using Virtual Functions).
- Exam Point: Polymorphism is essential for code reusability and flexibility.
